$comment: Practical guidance for planning any research article for ARO. Everything here is a recommendation, not an ARO rule, except where 'aro' lists requirement ids. No results are stated or implied: placeholders in examples are written as [X].
summary: A planning aid for any research article: for each manuscript section, what it is for, what evidence a reviewer expects, what to write, and when it is done. It is not tied to a field; adapt the wording to your own study.

sections.name: Title and index terms
sections.purpose: Tell a reader outside your subfield what you studied and how.
sections.evidence: None; it must match what the Results show.
content: Name the subject, the method or approach, and the setting or population.
Avoid acronyms in the title unless unavoidable.
Choose index terms a reader would search for, not just words from the title.
sections.example: [Method] for [Problem] in [Setting]: [A Comparison / A Case Study / An Evaluation] (aim for 15 words or fewer).

sections.name: Abstract
sections.purpose: Let the editor decide in one read whether the paper is worth reviewing.
sections.evidence: Only findings that appear in Results, with the same numbers.
content: Why: the problem and the gap, in one or two sentences.
What and how: what you did and the main method.
Findings: your two or three main results, with numbers.
Significance: what a reader should do or believe differently.
sections.example: [Problem] matters because [reason], yet [gap]. We [method] on [data/setting] and compare it with [baseline]. [Main result with a number]. This suggests [implication] …

sections.name: Introduction
sections.purpose: Show the gap and state the contribution, with no subheadings.
sections.evidence: Citations to peer-reviewed work that establishes the problem and what earlier studies did and did not cover.
content: The problem and why it matters.
What earlier work has done, and the specific gap it leaves.
What this paper does about the gap.
A short list of contributions, each pointing to a result.
sections.example: Contributions: (1) [what is new]; (2) [what is shown or measured]; (3) [what is released or recommended].

sections.name: Materials and Methods
sections.purpose: Let another team reproduce every number.
sections.evidence: Data or material descriptions, procedures, exact settings, and definitions of every measure.
content: Data or materials: source, licence or permission, size, and any cleaning or exclusions.
Procedure: the steps, tools and versions, parameters and random seeds.
Design: the conditions, groups or configurations you compared.
Baselines or controls, and why you chose them.
Measures, defined as numbered equations where they are mathematical.
Ethics approval or consent, where people or animals are involved.
Equipment or compute used.
sections.example: The error rate is the share of wrong predictions: E = N_wrong / N   (1), where N_wrong is the number of incorrect predictions and N the number of test cases.
done: Every dataset has a source, licence and size
Settings are enough to repeat the work

sections.name: Results and Discussion
sections.purpose: Report what happened, then explain it.
sections.evidence: Tables and figures for every comparison claimed; variance, confidence intervals or significance where you claim a difference.
content: Main results, one question at a time.
Comparison with baselines or earlier work.
Examples or error analysis that explain the numbers.
What the results mean and what they do not show.
Limitations: data coverage, assumptions, measures that miss something.
sections.example: Figure titles that state the finding: 'Fig. 3. Accuracy rises with training size, flattening after [X]'.
done: Every claim cites a figure or table
Within the figure cap for your word band

sections.name: Conclusions
sections.purpose: State what a reader should take away, and what comes next.
content: Main findings in a few sentences.
A practical recommendation, if one follows from the results.
Future work.

sections.name: Acknowledgment
sections.purpose: Credit funding, resources and help; disclose interests.
content: Funding and grants.
Equipment, compute or facility providers.
Data providers and contributors who are not authors.
Conflicts of interest, if any.
sections.example: The authors thank [...] for access to [...].
done: Omitted from the anonymised copy if it identifies you

sections.name: References
content: Harvard author-date, alphabetical.
Peer-reviewed versions of every paper you cite.
DOIs or URLs.
Datasets and software cited where their licence asks.

topics.name: A clearly stated problem and gap
topics.note: Say what is not yet known or not yet solved, with citations, before saying what you did.

topics.name: Related work
topics.note: Cover the closest earlier studies fairly, including ones that disagree with you.

topics.name: Data or materials
topics.note: Source, size, permissions or licences, and what was excluded and why.

topics.name: Method and design
topics.note: Enough detail, versions and settings that another team can repeat the work.

topics.name: Baselines and controls
topics.note: Name what you compared against and how you obtained it; choose it before seeing results.

topics.name: Measures and evaluation
topics.note: Define each measure, ideally as a numbered equation, and use the same test data for every comparison.

topics.name: Statistical analysis and variability
topics.note: Repeated runs, confidence intervals or tests wherever you claim one result beats another.

topics.name: Which part matters
topics.note: Where the method has several parts or settings, show what happens when each is changed or removed.

topics.name: Cost and efficiency
topics.note: Time, memory or resources used, with the hardware stated, where relevant.

topics.name: Examples and error analysis
topics.note: Show representative successes and failures, not only averages.

topics.name: How far the findings generalise
topics.note: State the conditions under which the result holds and where it was not tested.

topics.name: Ethics, consent and data protection
topics.note: Where people, animals or personal data are involved, state approvals and how data were protected.

topics.name: Limitations
topics.note: Be specific about assumptions, coverage and measures that do not capture everything.

topics.name: Reproducibility and availability
topics.note: Settings, seeds and data sources in the paper; release code and data where permissions allow, kept anonymous during review.

matrix.evidence: The same test data, the same measure, and the baseline's version and settings

matrix.claim: A setting of [X] is a good trade-off
matrix.evidence: Results across the whole range tried, plus the cost side of the trade-off
matrix.strength: Show the curve, not one point

matrix.evidence: Results for each level of the factor with everything else held fixed
matrix.strength: Same evaluation data for every level

matrix.evidence: Earlier approaches run on the same data, with versions named
Ablations or examples that isolate the mechanism
matrix.strength: Isolate one change at a time

matrix.claim: The finding generalises beyond our data
matrix.evidence: A second dataset, setting or population
matrix.strength: Without it, describe the claim as a hypothesis

matrix.evidence: Full settings, seeds, data sources and a code release plan
